**February 20, 1952 — Wednesday**

You arrived on a Wednesday in the cold middle of a pivotal winter — not merely a winter of weather, but a winter between eras.

---

**The Games Were On**

On the exact day of your birth, the VI Winter Olympics were underway in Oslo, Norway, where they had opened six days earlier. Oslo had hosted a Games it had quietly wanted for decades, and the Norwegian crowds were enormous and jubilant. Hjalmar Andersen of Norway was in the process of winning three speed skating gold medals — a performance that would define those Games in memory. You were born into a world mid-competition, mid-ceremony, mid-flag. There is something fitting about that: you entered a world already in motion.

**A Queen Fourteen Days Old**

Two weeks before your birth, on February 6th, King George VI died in his sleep at Sandringham. His daughter Elizabeth, 25 years old and on a royal tour of Kenya, was told she was now Queen. She flew home to a Britain still rationing food, still clearing rubble, still learning what peacetime meant. When you were born on February 20th, the new Queen's reign was exactly fourteen days old. Elizabeth II would reign for seventy years — longer than your entire childhood, adolescence, adulthood, and middle age combined. The crown she received that week would outlast most of the century's certainties.

**A War No One Wanted to Name**

The Korean War had been grinding for nineteen months. It was called a "police action" by the American government, a bureaucratic euphemism for a conflict that had already killed tens of thousands. The front lines had largely stabilized near the 38th parallel — roughly where they started — and peace negotiations were stalled at Panmunjom over prisoner exchanges. The war would drag on until July 1953. You were born into its middle, into a country debating the cost of commitments it hadn't quite chosen.

**Truman's Last Year**

Harry Truman was in the final year of his presidency, though the public didn't know it yet — he would announce in March that he wouldn't seek another term. His approval ratings were low, the war unpopular, the Washington scandals draining. By the time you were a few months old, Dwight Eisenhower had won the presidency in a landslide, beginning a Republican administration that would define the decade. The political world you were born into would change its character completely before your first birthday.

**The Hydrogen Shadow**

Nine months after your birth, in November 1952, the United States detonated Ivy Mike — the first true hydrogen bomb — on a Pacific atoll, reducing the island of Elugelab to a crater beneath the sea. The Soviet Union had already tested an atomic bomb in 1949. The Cold War you were born into was about to acquire a new and permanent quality: the permanent possibility of civilizational annihilation. This was the background radiation of your childhood, something your generation understood as children through drills and duck-and-cover films, and carried into adulthood as a sober condition of existence.

**What Ordinary Life Looked Like**

The house you were born into almost certainly had a radio at its center, not a television. Fewer than a third of American homes had a TV set in early 1952; by the time you started school, that fraction would reverse completely. A new car cost around $1,800. A first-class stamp cost three cents. Polio was still a terror — Jonas Salk's vaccine was three years away. Commercial air travel existed but was a luxury for the prosperous; most Americans who went anywhere went by train or car. The interstate highway system didn't exist yet; Eisenhower would sign it into law in 1956.

**The Lifetime That Followed**

You are 74 years old today — which means you have lived through a span of transformation that has few historical parallels. You were a child when Sputnik beeped overhead and rewrote the sky. You were a teenager when the first humans walked on the moon. You reached adulthood just as Watergate showed a democracy eating itself, and middle age just as the Soviet Union — the defining adversary of your entire first four decades — dissolved overnight. The internet arrived in your forties. The smartphone arrived in your fifties. Now, in your seventies, the systems doing the talking in this conversation didn't exist five years ago.

---

You were born into a world of radio, rationing, and atomic anxiety — a world that traveled by rail and communicated by letter, where the fastest computers occupied entire floors and performed calculations that a wristwatch now exceeds. The world you inhabit in 2026 would be genuinely unrecognizable to the people who waited in that hospital in February 1952. You are, by any measure, a person who has watched the world remake itself from scratch — not once, but several times.
